title: Rework azure-ephemeral CI to use a Nix devshell for the toolchain
description:
Follow-up to bd-f023df. Operator (Harry / router, 2026-06-28): the azure-ephemeral runners have Nix+flakes but NO bare toolchains on PATH (bare cargo is absent). Agents hit missing-toolchain failures. Fix: rework CI to enter a Nix devshell (nix develop .#<shell>) for the toolchain instead of installing it via an action or requiring a custom runner image.

For mcp-cli (which currently provisions rust via dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable and has no flake):
1. Add a flake.nix exposing devShells.default with the Rust toolchain (cargo, rustc, clippy, rustfmt) from nixpkgs; commit the generated flake.lock for reproducibility.
2. Rework .github/workflows/ci.yml: drop the dtolnay/rust-toolchain step; run each check under `nix develop --command cargo ...` (fmt --check, clippy -D warnings, test). Keep the job on runs-on [self-hosted, azure-ephemeral]; keep workflow_dispatch-only until mcp-cli is added to the runner pool repos list.

Validate locally with Nix (available here): nix flake lock; nix develop --command cargo fmt/clippy/test all green. Also confirm plain cargo still passes.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: Cover read_protocol_message framing error paths and write_json_result with tests
description:
The MCP message framing reader `read_protocol_message` has three error/robustness
paths with no test coverage:

- missing Content-Length header -> McpCliError::Protocol("missing Content-Length ...")
- invalid Content-Length value (non-numeric) -> Protocol("invalid Content-Length ...")
- unexpected EOF after headers began but before a blank line -> Protocol("unexpected EOF ...")

Additionally the owned `write_json_result` helper (as opposed to the already-used
`write_json_result_ref`) has no direct test.

These guard the JSON-RPC stdio transport against malformed client framing producing
panics instead of clean structured Protocol errors, and lock the owned envelope
writer's output shape.

Scope: test-only additions in src/lib.rs #[cfg(test)]. The framing reader is a
private fn, so tests live in the same module (already the case). No production code
changes expected. Keep generic.

Filed by mcp-cli-dev-aur-0 while progressing the lane.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: Drop the unused tracing dependency (never referenced since the crate extraction)
description:
## Problem

`Cargo.toml` declares `tracing = "0.1.41"`, but `src/lib.rs` contains zero
references to it. The dependency was introduced in the extraction commit
(bd-f9bf4d, `9e2f1fc`) and has never been used, so every consumer of `mcp-cli`
inherits `tracing`, `tracing-core`, and `pin-project-lite` for nothing.

Verify with:

    grep -c 'tracing' src/lib.rs   # 0

## Options

1. **Remove it** (preferred, matches the crate's "keep it minimal" design rule).
   Zero risk: the compiler proves nothing uses it, and at 0.0.1 there is no
   semver obligation.
2. Or deliberately wire it up. An MCP stdio server cannot log to stdout (stdout
   is the protocol channel), so `tracing` events on the protocol error paths
   (parse error, invalid request, unknown method, tool failure) would be the
   idiomatic way to give consumers observability. This is a bigger, opinionated
   change and should be its own bead with its own tests if wanted.

Unless someone wants option 2, take option 1.

## Acceptance criteria

- `tracing` removed from `Cargo.toml` (or used, if option 2 is chosen deliberately).
- `cargo fmt` / `clippy -D warnings` / `cargo test` stay green.
creator: ms-dev-3:mcp-cli:ms-dev-3-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md3-0

title: Cover MCP ping, initialized-notification, and unknown-method (-32601) paths with tests
description:
The stdio MCP server (`McpServer::handle_request`) implements several JSON-RPC
behaviors that currently have no test coverage:

- `ping` -> returns `{"result": {}}` with the request id.
- `notifications/initialized` -> returns no response (notification; id-less).
- unknown/unsupported method -> JSON-RPC error object with code `-32601` and an
  "unsupported MCP method" message.

Only initialize/tools.list/tools.call are exercised today (via
stdio_server_handles_initialize_list_and_call). Adding focused tests for ping,
the initialized notification (no reply), and the unknown-method error path locks
down protocol correctness and guards against regressions in the JSON-RPC framing
layer.

Scope: test-only additions in src/lib.rs #[cfg(test)] using the existing
frame_request / parse_framed_responses helpers. No production code changes
expected. Keep generic per crate constraints.

Filed by mcp-cli-dev-aur-0 while progressing the lane (operator: workers improve
projects).
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: MCP initialize should negotiate protocolVersion, not hardcode 2024-11-05
description:
Observed while implementing bd-909a82. In `McpServer::handle_request`, the `initialize` response hardcodes `"protocolVersion": "2024-11-05"` and ignores the `protocolVersion` the client sent in the initialize params. Per the MCP spec the server should echo back the client's requested protocol version when it can support it, and otherwise respond with a version it does support so the client can decide whether to proceed or disconnect. Hardcoding the oldest revision pins every session to 2024-11-05 even when a modern client (e.g. 2025-03-26 / 2025-06-18) connects; most clients will silently downgrade, but it is suboptimal and not spec-aligned negotiation.

Suggested fix: read the client's requested `protocolVersion` from initialize params, and respond with that value if it is in a small set of supported versions, otherwise fall back to the server's latest supported version (currently 2024-11-05). Keep the crate generic — supported-version set can be a const slice. Add a test asserting a known client version is echoed and an unknown one falls back.

File: src/lib.rs, `initialize` arm of `handle_request`. Filed via reflect-session mixin from bd-909a82 session.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: Tools with non-object input types advertise a spec-invalid MCP inputSchema
description:
MCP constrains `Tool.inputSchema` to a JSON Schema **object**: the spec's shape
is `{ "type": "object", "properties"?: {...}, "required"?: [...] }`.
`Tool::new_typed` derives the advertised schema with
`schemars::schema_for!(Input)` and pushes whatever comes back, with no check
that the root is an object.

Verified against the current crate by registering four tools and dumping
`tool_metadata()`:

- `Input = String`   -> `{"type":"string","title":"string"}`
- `Input = Vec<i64>` -> `{"type":"array","items":{...}}`
- `Input = enum`     -> `{"type":"string","enum":["Left","Right"]}`
- `Input = struct`   -> `{"type":"object",...}`  (correct)

So any consumer whose tool input is a scalar, sequence, enum, or newtype builds
a server that advertises invalid tool metadata. Strict MCP clients reject the
tool or the whole `tools/list` response. Nothing in mcp-cli says a word: the
mistake is made at registration and only surfaces later as a client-side
failure in someone else's process, which is the same silent-at-the-boundary
shape as bd-daeb00 (duplicate tool names).

Fix, mirroring the contract just landed for duplicate names:

- `try_add_tool` returns `Err(JsonError)` with code `invalid_input_schema`
  naming the tool and the offending root type; the router is left unchanged.
- `add_tool` (and the typed helpers that route through it) panics with the same
  message. Registration is startup-time, so this is a programming error that
  should fail immediately rather than ship invalid metadata.

Do NOT auto-wrap a scalar input into a synthetic object: that would silently
change the argument shape the handler receives and trade one invisible failure
for another. The consumer should declare a struct.

Out of scope, noted for separate triage: `schema_for!` also emits `$schema` and
uses `$defs`/`$ref` for nested types. Both are legal JSON Schema and the root
stays `type: object`, so this is conformant; some MCP clients do not resolve
`$ref`, but that is a client limitation, not a defect here.

Acceptance: a non-object input schema is rejected with `invalid_input_schema`
via the fallible path and panics via the ergonomic path; struct inputs
(including nested ones using `$defs`/`$ref`) still register; README documents
the constraint; fmt/clippy/tests green.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: The crate name mcp-cli is already taken on crates.io by an unrelated project, so this crate cannot be published as-is
description:
## Evidence

`https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/mcp-cli` resolves to a DIFFERENT project:

    registry name: mcp-cli
    registry desc: Interactive CLI debugger and TUI for MCP servers
    registry repo: https://github.com/conikeec/mcp-probe
    newest: 0.3.0 | downloads: 2308 | first published: 2025-06-21

Ours is `Reusable JSON envelope and MCP stdio helpers for CLI projects` at
`harryaskham/mcp-cli`. Same name, different crate, and the registry entry is
theirs. There are no git tags in this repo and no published version of our
crate under that name.

## Why it matters

`Cargo.toml` is dressed for publication and has been since the extraction:
`description`, `license`, `readme`, `keywords`, `categories`, `repository`,
`homepage`, `documentation`, and a `0.0.1` version. That is a crate someone
intended to publish. The intent is blocked and was not recorded anywhere, so
the metadata quietly implies a release story that cannot happen.

It also settles a question raised in bd-57c17b: since nothing is published,
nobody can pin by version, so consumption is by git rev or path/submodule and a
changelog is sufficient there. A version bump is an honest marker rather than a
consumer protection.

## Why it was not caught by the obvious check

`cargo publish --dry-run` passes cleanly here (12 files packaged and verified).
Dry-run packages and compiles locally; it never attempts the upload, so it
CANNOT detect a name collision. A green dry-run means "packages", not
"publishable". Worth knowing before anyone else uses it as evidence.

## Decision required (operator/owner, not a worker call)

1. Rename to a free name (`mcp-cli-core`, `mcp-cli-framework`, `cli-mcp`, ...)
   and keep the publication metadata meaningful.
2. Decide explicitly that this crate is git/submodule-consumed forever, and
   trim or annotate the publication metadata so it stops implying otherwise.

Either is fine; leaving it undecided is the bad option, because the next person
to try `cargo publish` discovers it at the upload step.

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision is recorded (rename, or explicitly git-consumed).
- If renamed: `Cargo.toml` name updated, README and profile references updated,
  name availability re-verified against crates.io before landing.
- If git-consumed: metadata trimmed or a note added saying why it is retained.

title: [broken-on-main] clippy too_many_lines on handle_request fails CI
description:
CI is failing on main. Two consecutive runs red:

    run 30604553493  bd-a9b422  FAILURE  2026-07-31T04:35Z
    run 30604669851  bd-cc4429  FAILURE  2026-07-31T04:38Z

Failure is `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D
warnings`:

    error: this function has too many lines (104/100)
       --> src/lib.rs:731:5
        |
    731 | /     fn handle_request(

`Cargo.toml` enables `clippy::pedantic` at warn with `-D warnings` in CI, so
`too_many_lines` is fatal there. `handle_request` crossed the 100-line limit
when bd-a9b422 added the notifications/initialized arm; bd-cc4429 then landed
on top of an already-red main.

Pre-existing relative to the tool-name work in bd-e6ed5d; not caused by it.

Contributing process failure, worth recording: after rebasing onto the other
worker's commit I re-ran `cargo test` but not `cargo clippy`. A rebase
invalidates a previous clippy run exactly as much as it invalidates a previous
test run, and the local smoke check has to be re-run against the actual rebased
tree, not the tree it was written on.

Fix: behaviour-preserving extraction of the `tools/call` arm out of
`handle_request` into its own method, where the bulk of the length is. Not a
`#[allow]`, and no change to message semantics.

Acceptance: clippy clean at `-D warnings`; all tests still pass; no behavioural
change to any JSON-RPC method arm; CI green on main.

title: Advertise tool outputSchema and optionally validate structuredContent (MCP 2025-06-18)
description:
MCP revision 2025-06-18 lets tools declare an `outputSchema` (JSON Schema for the tool's `structuredContent`) so clients can validate results. `mcp-cli` already returns `structuredContent` (the JsonEnvelope) from `tools/call`, but tool metadata (`ToolMetadata`) only carries `input_schema`; it does not advertise an output schema.

Potential enhancement: generate and advertise an `outputSchema` for each typed tool so clients can validate structured results, and optionally validate outgoing `structuredContent` against it in debug/test builds.

Why this is a draft (needs maintainer/operator decision, not a unilateral change): generating an accurate output schema requires adding an `Output: JsonSchema` bound to `Tool::new_typed` / `add_typed_tool`. That is an additive-but-breaking API change — every consumer's output type would need to derive `JsonSchema`. The envelope wrapper (`JsonEnvelope<Output>`) also complicates what exactly the advertised schema should describe (the raw Output vs the full success/error envelope). Decide the scope (raw output schema vs envelope schema; opt-in vs always-on) before implementing.

References: src/lib.rs `ToolMetadata`, `Tool::new_typed`, the `tools/call` arm of `handle_request`. Filed proactively during an idle burndown after closing bd-909a82 / bd-1bd8b6 / bd-e32020 / bd-b0314b.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: MCP server rejects JSON-RPC batches, but the advertised 2025-03-26 protocol version requires receiving them
description:
## Problem

`SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS` advertises `2025-03-26`, and that MCP revision
requires implementations to be able to RECEIVE JSON-RPC batches (an array of
request objects). Sending batches was optional; receiving them was not.

Today a batch array reaches `serde_json::from_value::<JsonRpcRequest>`, fails to
deserialize into a single request object, and is answered with a single
`-32600 Invalid Request`. A spec-conformant `2025-03-26` client that batches its
`initialize`/`tools/list` warm-up therefore gets one error instead of N
responses, and none of its calls run.

## Expected (JSON-RPC 2.0 section 6)

- A non-empty array is handled member-by-member; the server replies with an
  array of the responses, in the same order, OMITTING members that are
  notifications (no `id`).
- A batch consisting only of notifications produces NO response at all.
- An empty array is itself an Invalid Request and is answered with a single
  `-32600` object, not an array.
- A malformed member inside an otherwise valid batch gets its own `-32600`
  entry; the sibling members are still executed.
- The session keeps serving afterwards, consistent with the existing
  reconnect-safe contract.

## Notes

`2025-06-18` removed batching. Accepting batches unconditionally is the tolerant
choice and keeps the code simpler than version-gating the transport; clients on
`2025-06-18` simply never send them. Document that decision in the README.

## Acceptance criteria

- Batch requests are executed and answered as an array, ordered, notifications omitted.
- Notification-only batches produce no output frame.
- Empty batch returns a single `-32600`.
- Framed stdio tests cover ordering, notification omission, notification-only,
  empty batch, mixed valid/invalid members, and keep-serving.
- README documents batch handling and the version rationale.
- `cargo fmt` / `clippy -D warnings` / `cargo test` stay green.
creator: ms-dev-3:mcp-cli:ms-dev-3-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md3-0

title: 17 commits with breaking behavioural changes landed at 0.0.1 with no changelog and no version bump
description:
Seventeen commits landed on main on 2026-07-30/31. `version` is still 0.0.1,
unchanged throughout, and there is no CHANGELOG. A consumer pinning this crate
by path or git has no way to learn what moved under them short of reading the
log.

Several of the changes are behavioural, not additive. Inventory while the
context is fresh, because this is cheap for me to write now and expensive for
anyone to reconstruct later:

BEHAVIOURAL / BREAKING

- `add_tool` and the three typed helpers now PANIC where they previously
  accepted silently: duplicate tool name (bd-daeb00), non-object input schema
  (bd-2308cb), empty or whitespace-only name (bd-e6ed5d). A consumer whose
  registration hits any of these currently ships a broken server and will now
  fail at startup instead. That is the point, but it is a behaviour change at
  process start, which is the most disruptive place to meet one.
- `serve_transport` no longer returns `Err(McpCliError::Json)` on a malformed
  frame; it answers -32700 and keeps serving (bd-9171bc). Anyone matching on
  that Err arm is now dead code. The crate's own test asserting the old
  behaviour had to be re-pointed, so at least one caller existed.
- Handler panics no longer propagate out of `Tool::call`; they become an
  `isError` envelope with code `tool_panicked` (bd-c18590). A consumer relying
  on fail-fast process death now has a server that keeps running.
- Frames larger than `DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES` (16 MiB) are now rejected with
  -32700 (bd-bb6800). Previously any size was accepted given enough memory.
- Advertised `outputSchema` gained a root `"type": "object"` (bd-cc4429). A fix,
  but it is wire-visible metadata that a strict client may have been rejecting
  and will now accept - a behaviour change from the client's side.
- The `tracing` dependency was dropped (bd-0f31f3), removing it from the
  transitive graph for anyone who was relying on it arriving via this crate.

ADDITIVE

- `try_add_tool`, `DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES`, `McpServer::with_max_frame_bytes`,
  `McpServer::max_frame_bytes`.
- JSON-RPC batch receive (bd-55de1d).
- `notifications/initialized` carrying an id is now answered (bd-a9b422).
- Invalid UTF-8 on the transport no longer ends the session (bd-854d61).

The ask is not strict semver - 0.0.x explicitly permits breaking changes in a
patch release, so nothing here is a violation. The ask is that the changes be
RECORDED, so a consumer can upgrade deliberately rather than discovering the
panic-on-duplicate-registration at someone else's startup.

Options:

1. Add CHANGELOG.md in Keep a Changelog form, seeded with the above as an
   Unreleased section. Cheapest, and it makes the next entry someone's habit
   rather than an archaeology exercise.
2. As 1, plus bump to 0.0.2 and cut the section, so there is a version a
   consumer can actually pin to a described state. Slightly more ceremony, and
   it raises whether anyone is pinning at all - worth knowing either way.
3. Do nothing: the repo is young, the git log is the changelog, and a consumer
   reads it.

I lean 2 if any consumer pins by version and 1 if they all pin by git rev, and I
do not know which is true - that is genuinely a question for whoever owns the
release story rather than something I should assume. Filing as a draft rather
than picking.

Not in either worker's declared lane, which is likely why it went unnoticed
while both of us were auditing inside the code.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: Classify unknown-tool tools/call error as TargetNotFound, not Validation
description:
ToolRouter::call_tool returns an unknown-tool error with ErrorCategory::Validation (code "unknown_tool"). The ErrorCategory enum has a dedicated TargetNotFound variant that exists precisely for "the named target does not exist" — the same way a missing window id or file would be classified. Since the structured ErrorCategory is the framework's programmatic contract for routing/handling errors, a not-found condition surfacing as Validation (which is for malformed input) is a misclassification: consumers filtering on category cannot distinguish "you sent bad input" from "that tool name doesn't exist".

Fix: change the unknown-tool path in call_tool to ErrorCategory::TargetNotFound (code "unknown_tool" unchanged). The typed-input deserialization failure path stays Validation (that genuinely is bad input). Add a category assertion (target_not_found) to the existing stdio unknown-tool test. Pre-1.0 crate, so this small semantic refinement to error classification is acceptable. Run cargo fmt/clippy/test.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0
spoken_name: classify tool error target not found

title: MCP stdio: invalid UTF-8 on the transport ends the session (Io/InvalidData), same shape as the -32700 gap
description:
Observed while fixing bd-9171bc (malformed JSON frames now answered with -32700
instead of ending the session).

`read_protocol_message` (src/lib.rs) frames each message with
`reader.read_line(&mut line)` into a `String`. `BufRead::read_line` validates
UTF-8 and returns `Err(io::ErrorKind::InvalidData)` on a non-UTF-8 byte. That
error propagates through `serve_transport` / `serve_stdio` as
`McpCliError::Io` and terminates the session — the same "one bad byte from the
peer kills a long-lived server" shape that bd-909a82 (-32600/-32602) and
bd-9171bc (-32700) removed at the layers above, still live one layer down.

MCP does require stdio frames to be UTF-8, so rejecting the frame is correct;
ending the session is the part that is not. A peer that emits one corrupt byte
(binary noise, truncated multibyte write, a wrapper leaking non-UTF-8 log
output onto the same fd) loses every subsequent request.

Suggested fix: read the frame as bytes (`read_until(b'\n', &mut Vec<u8>)`),
then attempt UTF-8/JSON interpretation per frame. An invalid-UTF-8 frame
becomes a `-32700` parse error response (the id is unrecoverable, so null) and
the loop continues, exactly like the JSON case. Only genuine I/O failures on
the underlying reader should end the session.

Note this reshapes the same read loop as bd-bb6800 (unbounded line length):
`read_until` on a raw `Vec<u8>` is where a size cap would naturally live, so
the two are cheaper done together than separately.

Acceptance: a non-UTF-8 frame yields -32700 and does not end the session; a
valid request after it is still served; genuine I/O errors still propagate;
fmt/clippy/tests green.

Filed via reflect-session mixin from the bd-9171bc session.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: tools/call structuredContent must conform to advertised outputSchema (envelope mismatch)
description:
Spec-correctness bug in the opt-in outputSchema feature (bd-5221f5). `tools/call` always returns `structuredContent` = the full JsonEnvelope serialization (`{status, meta, data}` on success / `{status, meta, error}` on error). But `new_typed_with_output_schema` advertises `outputSchema = schema_for!(Output)` — the schema of the bare `data` payload only. MCP 2025-06-18 requires that when a tool declares an outputSchema, the returned structuredContent MUST conform to it. A spec-compliant client validating structuredContent against the advertised outputSchema would FAIL, because the envelope's top-level shape (status/meta/data) does not match the bare Output schema.

Fix (non-breaking; structuredContent shape is unchanged so existing consumers like tendril are unaffected): advertise the schema of the envelope that actually wraps Output. Derive JsonSchema for ErrorCategory, EnvelopeMeta, JsonError, and JsonEnvelope<T>, and set `output_schema = schema_for!(JsonEnvelope<Output>)`. This makes the advertised schema describe the real structuredContent (a tagged success/error envelope whose `data` matches Output).

Update the typed_tool_can_advertise_output_schema test to assert the envelope-shaped schema (status discriminator + data->Output), add coverage that a real tools/call structuredContent structurally matches the advertised schema, refresh the doc comment + README MCP section. Run cargo fmt/clippy/test.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: MCP stdio server tears down the session on invalid JSON instead of returning -32700 Parse error
description:
## Problem

`McpServer::serve_transport` currently propagates a `McpCliError::Json` (and
therefore ENDS the serve loop) whenever a line on the stdio transport is not
valid JSON. A single stray non-JSON line — a wrapper process logging to stdout,
a partially flushed write, a shell banner, a UTF-8 BOM — kills the entire MCP
session, so the client sees the server exit rather than an error it can skip.

This is the last remaining teardown hole in the reconnect-safe contract:
bd-909a82 already fixed malformed-but-parseable input (`-32600` Invalid Request,
`-32602` Invalid params) and bd-b22230 locked idempotent re-initialize, but
"parseable as a line, not parseable as JSON" still terminates the session.

The current behaviour is locked by the regression test
`stdio_server_rejects_non_json_input_instead_of_hanging`, which asserts
`Err(McpCliError::Json(_))`. That test's real intent was "must not hang"; the
teardown was the expedient way to satisfy it at the time.

## Expected

JSON-RPC 2.0 section 5.1 defines `-32700 Parse error` for "Invalid JSON was
received by the server", and MCP inherits it. The server should:

1. Emit a `-32700` JSON-RPC error response with `id: null` (the id cannot be
   recovered from unparseable text).
2. KEEP SERVING subsequent well-formed messages on the same transport.

## Acceptance criteria

- Non-JSON input produces a `-32700` error response, not a terminated session.
- A well-formed `tools/call` sent AFTER a garbage line is still answered.
- The existing regression test is updated (not deleted) to assert the new
  non-hanging, non-teardown contract.
- README MCP protocol section documents `-32700` alongside the other codes.
- `cargo fmt` / `clippy -D warnings` / `cargo test` stay green.
creator: ms-dev-3:mcp-cli:ms-dev-3-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md3-0

title: MCP stdio server should return JSON-RPC errors for invalid request / invalid params, not tear down the session
description:
A long-running MCP stdio server (McpServer::serve_transport) must keep serving across many requests on one connection. Today only `-32601 method not found` is handled gracefully; two other malformed-but-parseable cases instead propagate a Rust error out of `serve_transport`, terminating the entire session and dropping all subsequent valid requests:

1. A JSON value that parses but is not a valid JSON-RPC request (e.g. missing `method`): `handle_request_value` does `serde_json::from_value::<JsonRpcRequest>(request)?` which propagates. Per JSON-RPC 2.0 this should be `-32600 Invalid Request` (id recovered from the raw value if present, else null) and the server should keep running.
2. A `tools/call` with malformed `params` (e.g. missing `name`): `handle_request` does `serde_json::from_value::<ToolCallParams>(...)?` which propagates. Per JSON-RPC 2.0 this should be `-32602 Invalid params` with the request id, and the server should keep running.

Fix: handle both cases inside the request dispatch, returning the appropriate JSON-RPC error response object and continuing the serve loop. Add regression tests proving a session survives a bad message and still answers a following valid request.

Explicit non-goal (respecting bd-c7aeca): the non-JSON transport line case (`serde_json::from_slice` in `serve_transport`, exercised by `stdio_server_rejects_non_json_input_instead_of_hanging`) was deliberately made to fail visibly rather than hang. This bead does not change that interactive-garbage behavior; it only fixes the parseable-JSON cases. Whether non-JSON lines should also become `-32700` + continue is left as a separate operator decision.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: MCP stdio: malformed JSON line kills the session instead of returning -32700 Parse error
description:
`McpServer::serve_transport` (src/lib.rs) parses each framed line with
`serde_json::from_slice(&message)?`. A single line that is not valid JSON
therefore propagates `McpCliError::Json` out of `serve_transport` /
`serve_stdio` and terminates the stdio session.

Per JSON-RPC 2.0 (and the MCP stdio transport, which is newline-delimited
JSON-RPC), invalid JSON must be answered with a `-32700 Parse error`
response carrying `"id": null`, and a long-lived server should keep serving
subsequent messages.

This is the same defect class as the closed bd-909a82, which made invalid
*request objects* (`-32600`) and invalid *params* (`-32602`) non-fatal and
kept the session alive. The parse-error leg was never covered, so the layer
directly beneath those two fixes still tears the session down. One bad byte
from a buggy or noisy client kills an otherwise healthy server.

Current behaviour is pinned by the test
`stdio_server_rejects_non_json_input_instead_of_hanging` (src/lib.rs ~1373),
which asserts `Err(McpCliError::Json(_))`. That test was written to fix an
earlier hang; the error-return was an improvement over hanging but is not the
protocol-conformant outcome. It should be re-pointed at the `-32700` contract
while keeping the original "must not hang / must not silently consume"
property.

Acceptance:
- a malformed JSON line yields a `-32700` JSON-RPC error response with
  `"id": null` and does NOT end the session;
- a valid request following a malformed line is still served;
- the existing non-JSON regression test is updated (not deleted) to the new
  contract;
- fmt/clippy/tests green.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: Cover JsonEnvelope round-trip deserialize and initialize handshake completeness
description:
Two public-contract behaviors lack test coverage:

1. JsonEnvelope<T> round-trip deserialize. The envelope is a #[serde(tag="status")]
   tagged enum deriving Deserialize and is the crate's primary --json wire contract
   that consumers parse. Today only the serialize direction is tested; nothing proves
   the success and error variants deserialize back from their serialized JSON form
   (status tag dispatch, data/error payloads, meta).

2. initialize response completeness. The stdio initialize handler emits
   protocolVersion ("2024-11-05"), capabilities.tools.listChanged (false), and
   serverInfo.version (from StdioServerConfig.server_version), but the existing test
   only asserts serverInfo.name. A small assertion set locks the handshake shape.

Scope: test-only additions in src/lib.rs #[cfg(test)]. No production changes. Keep
generic. Locks the public CLI envelope contract bidirectionally and the MCP
initialize handshake.

Filed by mcp-cli-dev-aur-0 while progressing the lane.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: notifications/initialized sent with an id gets no response, stranding the client forever
description:
## Problem

`handle_request` matches `"notifications/initialized" => None` unconditionally,
discarding `request.id`. Every other arm respects the id: they use
`request.id.map(...)`, so a notification (no id) is silent and a request (id
present) gets a response.

JSON-RPC 2.0 defines a notification as a request object WITHOUT an id, and a
request that carries an id MUST be answered. A client that assigns an id to
every outgoing message — naive, but real — sends
`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":N,"method":"notifications/initialized"}` and then waits
forever for response N. The session is stalled with no error surfaced.

This is the same never-strand-the-peer failure class already hardened elsewhere:
bd-909a82 (invalid request/params), bd-9171bc (-32700 parse error), bd-b22230
(idempotent re-initialize), bd-bb6800/bd-854d61 (frame bounding).

## Expected

- No id present: stay silent (unchanged; this is the normal path).
- Id present: answer with an empty result, exactly as `ping` does. The method is
  being invoked as a request, so it gets a request's response rather than a
  `-32601`, which would misreport a method the server clearly supports.

## Acceptance criteria

- `notifications/initialized` with an id returns `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":N,"result":{}}`.
- `notifications/initialized` without an id still produces no frame at all
  (existing test must keep passing).
- Framed stdio test covers the id-present case and that the session keeps serving.
- `cargo fmt` / `clippy -D warnings` / `cargo test` stay green.
creator: ms-dev-3:mcp-cli:ms-dev-3-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md3-0

title: Assert crate-name availability in CI, because publish --dry-run is a control that cannot fire
description:
Recorded at operator-proxy request while resolving bd-26b8a3, so it is not
rediscovered. The rename fixes one instance; this removes the invisibility.

## The general problem

`cargo publish --dry-run` packages and compiles locally and NEVER attempts the
upload. It therefore cannot fail for the reason you care about when you run it:
it reported clean on this crate for however long the name has been taken, and it
would report clean the day before a real publish fails. Anyone treating it as
validation of publishability is holding a control that cannot fire.

This is the same shape as several other findings from 2026-07-31: a check that
returns a reassuring answer because it is structurally incapable of returning
the failing one.

## Sketch

A CI step that asserts the package name is either FREE or ALREADY OURS:

    NAME=$(cargo metadata --no-deps --format-version 1 | jq -r '.packages[0].name')
    CODE=$(curl -s -o body.json -w '%{http_code}' \
      -H "User-Agent: mcp-cli-core-ci" "https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/$NAME")
    # 404            -> free, pass
    # 200 + repository matches ours -> ours, pass
    # 200 + anything else           -> FAIL: name collision

Design notes for whoever takes it:

- Must tolerate crates.io being unreachable without failing the build; a
  network blip should not redden `main`. Warn-and-pass on non-200/404.
- Belongs on a schedule or on changes to `Cargo.toml`, not on every push \u2014 the
  answer changes rarely and it is an external call.
- The `repository` comparison is what distinguishes "ours" from "someone
  else's" once we do publish; match on the exact repository URL, not the name.

## Acceptance criteria

- CI fails when the package name is taken by a repository that is not ours.
- CI does not fail when crates.io is unreachable.
- Documented in the README or the workflow itself so the intent survives.
creator: ms-dev-3:mcp-cli:ms-dev-3-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md3-0

title: Document the MCP protocol surface (methods, version negotiation, error codes) in README
description:
The README documents JSON envelopes and tool registration but never describes the MCP stdio protocol surface the crate actually implements. Recent changes added public/behavioral surface that should be documented per the project profile's "Update README.md when public APIs or integration patterns change" rule:

- newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) stdio framing (bd-c7aeca)
- supported MCP methods: initialize (with protocol-version negotiation), ping, tools/list, tools/call, notifications/initialized
- the new pub const SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS and negotiation behavior (bd-1bd8b6)
- JSON-RPC error behavior that keeps the session alive: -32600 invalid request, -32601 method not found, -32602 invalid params (bd-909a82)

Add a concise "MCP protocol support" section to README.md covering these. Keep it generic (no consuming-project specifics). No code change; run fmt/clippy/test to confirm nothing regresses.

title: Lock MCP stdio reconnect-safe contract: idempotent repeated initialize keeps serving
description:
Operator (Harry, 2026-06-24) raised that a same-agent MCP reconnect can fail to be re-acknowledged in the cacophony precursor binary. Investigation confirms mcp-cli's McpServer is stateless per-message (holds only config+router; no per-connection/'already-initialized' state), so a repeated `initialize` on the same stdio stream is already answered idempotently and the session keeps serving. This bead locks that reconnect-safe contract with explicit regression tests so it stays the reference behavior the precursor should match:

1. Two `initialize` calls on the same serve_transport session both return a well-formed result (serverInfo + protocolVersion) and the session continues serving subsequent requests (e.g. a following ping/tools-list answered).
2. A re-`initialize` after `notifications/initialized` is still answered (no 'already initialized' rejection).

No production code change expected (documents/locks existing behavior); pure additive tests. Run cargo fmt/clippy/test.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: Switch mcp-cli reintegration to PR auto-merge (CI gate now live)
description: Harry directed (2026-06-29, via sgu24:nix-on-droid): switch to PR mode rather than relying on flaky direct checkouts; prefer PR auto-merge when available. mcp-cli now qualifies: hosted CI gate is green on push+PR (bd-bcb4b8), legs 1+2 enabled, and branch protection on main now requires the 'check' context (strict, enforce_admins=false escape hatch). Update the profile so pr_auto_merge is the default reintegration mode (direct kept as documented escape hatch). Dogfood by landing this very change via --mode pr_auto_merge.

title: Harden read_protocol_message against unbounded line length
description:
Observed during a reflect-session audit of src/lib.rs (post-burndown, board drained).

`read_protocol_message` (src/lib.rs) frames NDJSON by calling `reader.read_line(&mut line)` in a loop with no upper bound on line length. A single pathological/oversized line (no embedded newline) would be buffered entirely in memory, an unbounded allocation. Today the stdin peer is the agent's own trusted MCP client, so the practical risk is low and this is hardening, not a live bug.

Suggested fix: cap the accepted frame size with a configurable/default max (e.g. read via `reader.take(MAX).read_line(...)` or a manual byte loop), and on overflow return a structured framing error (McpCliError::Protocol or a JSON-RPC error that keeps the session serving, consistent with the existing invalid-request/-32600 handling) rather than allocating without limit. Add a test that a frame exceeding the cap is rejected cleanly and the session keeps serving the next valid request.

Acceptance: bounded read with a sensible default cap; clean rejection (no panic, no session teardown) on overflow; unit test covering the overflow path; clippy/fmt/tests stay green.

Filed via reflect-session mixin from the mcp-cli post-burndown idle audit (no anchor bead; board was fully drained).
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

description: Harry's auto-merge cutover: legs 1+2 (allow_auto_merge + allow_update_branch) already enabled on harryaskham/mcp-cli. Merge queue needs a GitHub org (mcp-cli is a personal-account repo) so it's unavailable for now — proceed with the tools we have. Leg 3 = a required GREEN CI check so auto-merge gates. mcp-cli CI was workflow_dispatch-only targeting a self-hosted azure-ephemeral pool (0 runners). Repo is public, so switch the CI job to GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest and trigger on pull_request + push to main (also merge_group for future MQ). Keep the existing cargo fmt/clippy/test validation (rust-not-nix via dtolnay). After it lands + runs once, require the check context in branch protection (strict). Operator green-lit proceeding.

title: Decide whether a panicking tool handler should kill the server process (it does today)
description:
Measured, not inferred. Registered two tools, sent two framed tools/call
requests in one stream - the first to a handler that panics, the second to a
handler that does not - and ran serve_transport over it:

    thread 'main' panicked at 'tool handler blew up'
    <process dies>

serve_transport never returns, no response frame is written for either request,
and the second tool is never invoked. A panic in one consumer-supplied closure
takes down the whole server process.

This is the same never-strand-the-peer family as bd-909a82 (-32600/-32602),
bd-9171bc (-32700), bd-bb6800/bd-854d61 (framing) and bd-a9b422
(notifications-with-id), but with a much larger blast radius: those stranded one
request or one session, this ends the process and every pending request with it.

Whether it is a DEFECT is a real design question, which is why this is a draft.
The argument each way:

- Rust convention says panics are bugs and libraries should not swallow them. A
  panicking handler is a defect in the consumer's code, and hiding it makes that
  defect harder to find.
- Against that: this crate exists to host third-party closures in a long-lived
  stdio server. That is the web-framework position, not the library position,
  and the web frameworks all landed on catching - axum/tower ships
  CatchPanicLayer, actix catches per-request - precisely because one handler
  bug should not take down a server serving everything else.

Options:

1. Do nothing, document it. A handler panic is process death; consumers must not
   panic. Cheapest, and honest, but it leaves the crate's most severe failure
   mode undocumented AND unguarded.
2. catch_unwind around the handler in Tool::call, converting a panic into an
   envelope error - ErrorCategory::ExecutionFailure, code `tool_panicked` - so
   the tool call fails, isError is true, and the session keeps serving. Needs
   AssertUnwindSafe because the handler is behind a &dyn Fn, and it is worth
   stating plainly that it does NOTHING under panic = "abort", so it is a
   mitigation and not a guarantee.
3. Opt-in via something like ToolRouter::catch_handler_panics(true), leaving the
   default as today. Preserves current behaviour for anyone relying on
   fail-fast, at the cost of the safe path being the one nobody selects.

My preference is 2 with the abort caveat documented. It matches what this crate
has now decided four separate times - report the failure at the boundary where
it happened and keep serving - and the isError envelope is exactly the right
shape for "your tool blew up", since it reaches the client as a tool-level
failure rather than a dead pipe.

Applying md3-0's test from bd-e6ed5d: is this a router invariant or somebody
else's constraint? I read it as ours. The router chose to hold consumer closures
behind Arc<dyn Fn> and invoke them inside a serve loop it owns; having taken
ownership of the call site, staying alive across a call is its contract, not the
consumer's. But that is the argument to attack if you disagree.

Not filing this as a bead because option 1 is genuinely defensible and I do not
want to pick unilaterally on something that changes behaviour for every existing
consumer.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: stdio transport must use newline-delimited JSON (MCP), not Content-Length framing
description:
mcp-cli's stdio transport uses LSP-style Content-Length header framing
(read_protocol_message / write_protocol_message), but the MCP stdio transport
specification uses newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON): each JSON-RPC message is a
single line terminated by \n, with no framing headers and no embedded newlines.

Impact: any real MCP client (e.g. `tendril mcp` / `tendril mcp stdio`) sends an
initialize request as a single newline-terminated JSON line with NO
Content-Length header. The server's read loop treats that JSON as a header line,
never finds the expected Content-Length + blank-line terminator, and blocks
reading more "headers" — so it never parses the request and never responds. The
client hangs in "connecting" forever. Operator reports all mcp-cli apps get
stuck connecting under tendril mcp.

Root cause masked by tests: every test (frame_request / parse_framed_responses)
speaks the server's own Content-Length dialect, so all 19 pass while real MCP
clients fail.

Fix: replace Content-Length framing with newline-delimited JSON on both read and
write paths:
- read: read one line, trim trailing \r\n, skip blank lines, parse the line as a
  full JSON-RPC message; EOF -> None.
- write: serialize compact JSON (no embedded newlines) + a single trailing \n,
  flush.
- Update test helpers and assertions to NDJSON. Keep the public serve_stdio /
  serve_transport signatures stable.

Scope: src/lib.rs production framing + tests. P1-ish correctness bug but filed as
task P2.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: Advertised outputSchema has no root type:object, so it is not a valid MCP outputSchema
description:
MCP 2025-06-18 constrains `Tool.outputSchema`, like `inputSchema`, to a JSON
Schema with a top-level `"type": "object"`
(https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/schema).

`Tool::new_typed_with_output_schema` advertises
`schemars::schema_for!(JsonEnvelope<Output>)`. Because `JsonEnvelope` is an
internally-tagged enum, schemars roots that schema in `oneOf` with NO top-level
`type`. Measured on the current crate, the advertised `outputSchema` is:

    {
      "$schema": "...",
      "$defs": { "Out": {...}, "EnvelopeMeta": {...}, "JsonError": {...} },
      "description": "Structured success/error envelope ...",
      "oneOf": [ {success variant, type:object}, {error variant, type:object} ],
      "title": "JsonEnvelope"
    }

Both branches are objects and both success and error `structuredContent`
validate against it, so bd-870183's conformance fix holds. The problem is one
level up: the schema document itself is not a valid MCP `outputSchema`, because
the root never declares `type`. A client validating tool metadata against the
MCP schema rejects the tool — or the whole `tools/list` response.

Note this is NOT caught by the bd-2308cb registration guard, deliberately: that
check only rejects a root which *declares* a non-object `type`, and this root
declares none. The conservative rule is still right for consumer-supplied input
types; the envelope schema is our own output and should simply be generated
correctly.

Fix: after deriving the envelope schema, insert `"type": "object"` at the root
when absent. `type` and `oneOf` are sibling keywords and both must hold, and
every valid envelope IS an object, so this rejects nothing that was previously
accepted while satisfying the spec. Do not flatten the `oneOf` into a permissive
object schema — that would throw away the success/error discrimination that
makes the envelope worth advertising.

Acceptance: the advertised outputSchema has a root `"type": "object"`; the
`oneOf` discrimination is preserved; success and error structuredContent both
still conform; fmt/clippy/tests green.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: Cover stdio tools/call error path (isError=true) end-to-end
description:
The stdio tools/call handler returns isError=true with the structured error
envelope embedded in structuredContent when a tool call fails, but only the
success path (isError=false) is tested today
(stdio_server_handles_initialize_list_and_call asserts isError==false).

The error half of the most important MCP operation is uncovered end-to-end
through the framing layer:

- tools/call for an unknown tool name -> isError=true, structuredContent.status
  == "error", error.code == "unknown_tool" (router emits "unknown tool `name`").
- tools/call with arguments that fail typed validation -> isError=true,
  structuredContent carries the validation error category/code.

A regression here would silently stop surfacing errors to MCP clients. Adding a
focused stdio test locks isError propagation and the embedded error envelope shape.

Scope: test-only additions in src/lib.rs #[cfg(test)] using existing
frame_request/parse_framed_responses helpers and build_math_router. No production
changes. Keep generic.

Filed by mcp-cli-dev-aur-0 while progressing the lane.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: ToolRouter silently accepts duplicate tool names, making the second registration unreachable
description:
`ToolRouter::add_tool` (src/lib.rs) pushes into a `Vec<Tool<Ctx>>` with no
uniqueness check, so registering the same tool name twice is silently accepted.

Two consequences, neither diagnosed anywhere:

- `tool_metadata()` / `tools/list` advertises the duplicate name twice. MCP
  clients key tools by name, so duplicate entries are malformed metadata and
  client behaviour is undefined (overwrite, error, or a visible dupe).
- `call_tool` uses `.find(..)`, so it dispatches to the FIRST registration
  forever. The second registration is unreachable dead code, and the consumer
  gets no warning at registration time or call time.

This is easy to hit in exactly the situation the crate is designed for: a
consuming CLI whose tool registration is spread across modules, or a rename
that updated one call site and not another. The failure is invisible until
someone notices a tool behaving like its older twin.

Fix: make the collision loud at registration time.

- `try_add_tool(&mut self, tool) -> Result<(), JsonError>` — structured
  rejection with code `duplicate_tool_name`, router left unchanged. For
  routers assembled dynamically from config/plugins.
- `add_tool` panics on duplicate with the offending name. Registration is a
  startup-time concern and a duplicate is a programming error, so failing
  loudly there is the point (same contract as axum panicking on overlapping
  routes). The typed helpers route through `add_tool` and inherit it.

Acceptance: duplicate registration is rejected with `duplicate_tool_name` via
the fallible path and panics via the ergonomic path; the router is unchanged
after a rejection and the original tool still dispatches; distinct names still
register; README documents both paths; fmt/clippy/tests green.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: CHANGELOG has no entry for the package rename, the one change that requires downstream action
description:
`CHANGELOG.md` has no entry for the package rename (bd-26b8a3, db4c2d1). The
header prose mentions it in passing, as the explanation for why entries are
keyed by commit, but the Changed section does not record it.

That is the most consumer-visible change in the crate's history. Every other
entry describes behaviour a consumer meets at runtime; this one changes the
dependency key in their Cargo.toml, so it is the single entry a reader scanning
for "what do I have to edit" needs to find. It is also the only change so far
that requires downstream action rather than merely rewarding attention.

Worth stating how it went missing, because it is not carelessness in either
direction. I wrote the changelog against the history as it stood; md3-0 landed
the rename shortly after and correctly updated the header prose to reflect the
new reality. Neither of us added the entry, because from each side it looked
like the other's artefact: I had finished my bead, and they were amending a file
someone else had just authored. The gap is exactly the seam problem again, one
scale down - a shared artefact edited by two owners in sequence, where the part
that needs changing is not the part either was looking at.

Fix: add a Changed entry naming the old and new package names, the fact that
the LIBRARY name is unchanged, and the one-line downstream remedy - rename the
dependency key, or keep it and add `package = "mcp-cli-core"`. The second form
matters: it means a rename that could have been source-breaking is not, and a
reader should not have to work that out.

Acceptance: the rename appears as a Changed entry citing bd-26b8a3 and db4c2d1;
the entry states that `use mcp_cli::...` paths are unaffected; both downstream
remedies are shown.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: McpCliError::category() always returns SerializationError for every variant
description:
`McpCliError::category()` (src/lib.rs) unconditionally returns `ErrorCategory::SerializationError` for every variant, including `Io(io::Error)` and `Protocol(String)`. Any consumer that projects a transport/CLI error into a JsonError via this category therefore mislabels I/O failures and protocol violations as serialization errors.

Fix: match on the variant and map to an appropriate category:
- `Io(_)` -> `ExecutionFailure` (transport I/O failure)
- `Json(_)` -> `SerializationError`
- `Protocol(_)` -> `Validation` (protocol/message violated expectations)

Keep the method a `const fn` (match is const-fn-legal). Add a unit test asserting each variant maps to its category.
creator: aurora:mcp-cli:aurora-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-aur-0

title: Decide how strict tool-name validation should be (empty names register today)
description:
Observed while finishing the registration-guard family (bd-daeb00 duplicate
names, bd-2308cb non-object input schemas, bd-cc4429 outputSchema root type).

`ToolRouter` accepts any `String` as a tool name. An empty name, a name with
spaces, or one with punctuation registers happily and is advertised in
`tools/list`.

MCP itself does not constrain the name charset, which is why I did not just add
this to the guard alongside the other two. But tool names routinely flow
onward into LLM function-calling APIs that DO constrain them — OpenAI's
function-name rule is effectively `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$` — so a name that is
legal by MCP can still make a downstream host reject the whole tool list. An
empty name is broken by any reading.

The design question, which is why this is a draft rather than a bead: should a
deliberately spec-minimal framework enforce a constraint the spec does not
state? Three defensible answers:

1. Reject only the indefensible: empty or whitespace-only names. Small, no
   opinion imported, catches the actual bug.
2. Reject anything outside `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`, matching the strictest
   common downstream consumer. Safest in practice, but bakes one vendor's rule
   into a generic crate.
3. Leave it alone and document the constraint in the README so consumers choose
   names that survive the whole pipeline.

My preference is 1 plus 3: reject empty/whitespace via the existing
`try_add_tool` / `add_tool` split with code `invalid_tool_name`, and document
the charset expectation without enforcing it. Wanted a triage decision rather
than picking unilaterally, since unlike the other three this one is a matter of
taste rather than a spec violation.

Filed via reflect-session mixin from the mcp-cli bd-cc4429 slice.
creator: ms-dev-4:mcp-cli:ms-dev-4-mcp-cli-mcp-cli-dev-md4-0

title: Nothing warns that stdout is the protocol channel: a println in a handler corrupts the stream
description:
## Measured, not asserted

Built a consumer against this crate whose tool handler does the single most
common thing a handler does wrong — `println!` — and ran `serve_stdio` with a
piped stdin/stdout. What the client receives:

    line 1: *** NOT JSON *** -> 'DEBUG: about to do work'
    line 2: VALID JSON-RPC   -> {"id":1,"jsonrpc":"2.0","result":{...}}

The debug line lands in the protocol stream, ahead of the response, as its own
frame. Nothing in the crate prevents, detects, or warns about it.

## Why it matters more than it looks

For an MCP stdio server, stdout IS the transport. Any `println!`, any dependency
that logs to stdout, any stray `dbg!` left in a handler silently corrupts the
session. It is the number one operational footgun of stdio MCP servers and the
crate is currently silent about it.

There is an irony worth noting: thanks to bd-9171bc this crate would SURVIVE
being on the receiving end of that garbage line — it answers `-32700` and keeps
serving. Most MCP clients are less forgiving and treat unparseable server output
as fatal. So the crate is hardened against other people's noise while giving its
own consumers no warning about producing it.

## Scope: documentation, deliberately

The tempting fix — redirecting fd 1 for the duration of `serve_stdio` — needs
`dup2`, and this crate sets `unsafe_code = "forbid"`. Detection is not portably
possible either. So the honest and sufficient fix is to say so, loudly, where a
consumer will read it:

- `serve_stdio` / `serve_transport` doc comments: stdout is the protocol
  channel; the consumer's own logging must go to stderr, including any
  `tracing`/`log` subscriber, which must be configured for stderr explicitly.
- README: same warning next to the protocol section, with the concrete symptom
  (client sees a non-JSON frame / drops the session) so it is searchable by the
  symptom rather than only by the cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- `serve_stdio` and `serve_transport` carry the warning in their doc comments.
- README documents it with the observable symptom.
- No behavioural change, no new dependency, no `unsafe`.
- `cargo fmt` / `clippy -D warnings` / `cargo test` stay green.

title: Add GitHub Actions CI on azure-ephemeral self-hosted runner
description:
Operator (Harry, 2026-06-28) directive: bring every project's CI onto the new azure-ephemeral self-hosted GitHub runners via `runs-on: [self-hosted, azure-ephemeral]`; one agent per project applies it. mcp-cli currently has NO CI at all (no .github/ directory), so this establishes minimal CI from scratch rather than retagging existing workflows.

Add `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with a single `check` job on `runs-on: [self-hosted, azure-ephemeral]`, triggered on push + pull_request to main, that mirrors the crate's existing local validation: cargo fmt --all -- --check; cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings; cargo test --workspace --all-features. Use dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable (components rustfmt, clippy) so the runner has the toolchain regardless of image (edition 2024 / MSRV 1.85). Validate locally with fmt/clippy/test (adding the workflow file does not affect the cargo build).

title: Add runnable doctest for README minimal pattern (0 doctests today)
description:
The README "Minimal pattern" section shows a `rust` fenced code block demonstrating
ToolRouter + McpServer usage, but it is not compiled or run as a doctest. `cargo test
--workspace --all-features` reports `Doc-tests mcp_cli ... 0 tests`, so the public
example is never verified against the real API and can silently rot as the surface
evolves.

Suggested fix shape: add a crate-level `//!` doc comment in `src/lib.rs` containing the
same minimal example as a runnable doctest (mirroring the README), or convert the README
block into a tested example. Keep the example generic per the crate's design constraint.
This gives compile-time protection for the documented entry-point pattern.

Observed during autonomous health-check of mcp-cli (check/test/clippy all green, 7 unit
tests pass, 0 doctests). Filed via reflect-session mixin from mcp-cli-dev-aur-0 idle
session.

bead.title: CHANGELOG has no entry for the package rename, the one change that requires downstream action
bead.description:
`CHANGELOG.md` has no entry for the package rename (bd-26b8a3, db4c2d1). The
header prose mentions it in passing, as the explanation for why entries are
keyed by commit, but the Changed section does not record it.

That is the most consumer-visible change in the crate's history. Every other
entry describes behaviour a consumer meets at runtime; this one changes the
dependency key in their Cargo.toml, so it is the single entry a reader scanning
for "what do I have to edit" needs to find. It is also the only change so far
that requires downstream action rather than merely rewarding attention.

Worth stating how it went missing, because it is not carelessness in either
direction. I wrote the changelog against the history as it stood; md3-0 landed
the rename shortly after and correctly updated the header prose to reflect the
new reality. Neither of us added the entry, because from each side it looked
like the other's artefact: I had finished my bead, and they were amending a file
someone else had just authored. The gap is exactly the seam problem again, one
scale down - a shared artefact edited by two owners in sequence, where the part
that needs changing is not the part either was looking at.

Fix: add a Changed entry naming the old and new package names, the fact that
the LIBRARY name is unchanged, and the one-line downstream remedy - rename the
dependency key, or keep it and add `package = "mcp-cli-core"`. The second form
matters: it means a rename that could have been source-breaking is not, and a
reader should not have to work that out.

Acceptance: the rename appears as a Changed entry citing bd-26b8a3 and db4c2d1;
the entry states that `use mcp_cli::...` paths are unaffected; both downstream
remedies are shown.
